name: Space Heater
blurb: Portable electric space heaters draw a lot of power for their size — a typical unit runs at 1,500 watts on high, the maximum a standard outlet safely supplies. Running one all evening is one of the fastest ways to inflate a winter electric bill.
tips: Heat only the room you're in and lower the central thermostat — a space heater loses money if the furnace keeps running too.
Use the built-in thermostat or a smart plug schedule instead of running it continuously.
A 750 W low setting costs exactly half as much per hour as the 1,500 W high setting.

name: Electric Furnace
blurb: Electric resistance furnaces are among the most expensive ways to heat a home. With 10–20 kW elements, even a few hours of runtime a day dominates a winter bill, which is why heat pumps typically cut that cost by half to two-thirds.
tips: Seal ducts and add attic insulation first — every leaked kWh from a resistance furnace is full price.
If you're on resistance heat, a heat pump upgrade usually has the fastest payback of any home energy project.
Lower the thermostat a few degrees at night; with resistance heat the savings are close to proportional.

name: Heat Pump
blurb: A heat pump moves heat instead of generating it, delivering two to four units of heat per unit of electricity. The compressor typically draws 1–5 kW, and total cost depends heavily on climate — cold snaps push it toward backup resistance strips.
tips: Avoid big thermostat setbacks — recovery can trigger expensive auxiliary resistance heat.
Keep the outdoor unit clear of snow, leaves, and shrubs; restricted airflow raises consumption.
Replace filters monthly in heavy season — a clogged filter can add 5–15% to runtime.

name: Baseboard Heater
blurb: Electric baseboard heaters are pure resistance heat: every watt in is a watt of heat out, at full retail price. A typical 6-foot unit draws about 1,500 watts, and homes heated entirely by baseboards often see the highest winter bills of any heating type.

name: Oil-Filled Radiator Heater
blurb: Oil-filled radiators feel gentler than fan heaters, but the physics is identical: 1,500 watts of resistance heat costs exactly the same regardless of the technology wrapped around it. Their advantage is steady, quiet heat — not lower bills.

name: Infrared Heater
blurb: Infrared heaters warm people and objects directly rather than the air, which can let you feel comfortable at a lower room temperature. Per hour of runtime, though, they cost the same as any resistance heater of equal wattage.

name: Electric Wall Heater
blurb: Recessed wall heaters with a fan are common in bathrooms, apartments, and additions. Typical units draw 1,000–2,000 watts, and because they're often on a wall thermostat, actual runtime — not rated wattage — decides the bill.

name: Garage Heater
blurb: Hardwired 240 V garage heaters commonly draw 5,000–7,500 watts — three to five space heaters' worth. Heating an uninsulated garage is expensive enough that insulation and door seals usually save more than any heater upgrade.

name: Electric Fireplace
blurb: An electric fireplace is a 1,400-watt space heater with better lighting. The flame effect alone uses just 5–10 watts, so running visuals without heat costs almost nothing — the heat setting is what shows up on your bill.

name: Electric Blanket
blurb: Electric blankets are one of the cheapest forms of warmth in the house — warming a person costs a tiny fraction of warming a room. Running one all night typically uses about a tenth the electricity of a space heater on low.

name: Heating Pad
blurb: A heating pad draws about as much power as an old light bulb, and typical sessions last under an hour. Even daily use costs well under a dollar a month in every state.

name: Pellet Stove
blurb: A pellet stove's heat comes from pellets, but the auger, igniter, and blower still draw 200–500 watts of electricity for hours at a time — a real, often-overlooked line on the winter bill of pellet-heated homes.

name: Furnace Blower Fan (Gas Furnace)
blurb: Even a gas furnace shows up on your electric bill: the blower fan that circulates air draws 300–800 watts whenever it runs. Older PSC motors cost several times more to run than modern ECM variable-speed motors doing the same job.

name: Radiant Floor Heating (Electric)
blurb: Electric radiant floor mats draw roughly 8–12 watts per square foot, so a large heated bathroom floor is effectively a space heater under the tile. A floor thermostat with a schedule is the difference between a small luxury and a large bill.

name: Engine Block Heater
blurb: Block heaters keep engine coolant warm on frigid nights, typically drawing 400–1,500 watts. A timer that switches it on two to three hours before you leave captures nearly all the benefit at a fraction of the all-night cost.
